newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee jumps to new highs on supply woes.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee jumps to new highs on supply woes.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures rocketed to new life of contract highs across-the-board on Thursday, as ongoing concerns about tight prompt supplies fueled a speculative buying spree, market sources said.

"There is not the amount of coffee needed and the market is showing that," said Christian Wolthers, vice president of Blaser & Wolther Specialty Trading Co, a Miami-based importer of green coffee. "People want to receive coffee and there's not enough coffee to deliver."

The spot May contract, which expires in 2-1/2 weeks, once again led the rally. May settled up a hefty 13.70 cents, to 252.05, after vaulting to a new contract high of 255.00 cents -- its highest intraday level since July 1994, when two devasting frosts hit top-grower Brazil.

Benchmark July arabicas soared 12.50 cents per lb -- or nearly six percent -- to finish at 222.90 cents, after ranging between a new lifetime high of 224.00 and 210.00 cents. The back months closed 3.25 to 9.85 higher.

Traders and analysts attributed the market's recent explosion -- which has seen the May contract surge 36.40 cents or about 17 percent since last Friday -- to a drawdown in stocks of coffee certified for delivery against the exchange.

After building to more than 83,000 60-kg bags three weeks ago, the CSCE reported after Wednesday's close that certified coffee stocks stood at 47,668 bags -- or the equivalent of about 168 lots -- as of April 29.
Meanwhile, open interest on the May contract was still relatively high at 1,719 lots.
"We have a May delivery situation which is really tight," said Dean Witter anaylst Steve Platt. "And we're not seeing the scale of producer selling because they are already pretty well sold."
Reflecting the lack of nearby availability, the May/July switch continued to widen today, ending at 29.85 from 28.65 at the close on Wednesday.
Many operators expect low consumer inventories and the approaching Brazilian frost season to keep coffee prices buoyant in the coming months.

Additionally, smaller-than-expected harvests in many Latin American countries -- most notably second-largest producer Colombia -- and the prospect of a smaller crop in top-grower Brazil in the 1997/98 season will underpin prices, they said.

"In the near-term, it's a clear situation of a shortage of deliverable coffee," said Wolthers. "In the medium term, it still looks very tight because there are no stocks in consuming countries and I don't see the promise of more coming in the pipeline. But in the longer term - a year to a year-and-a-half -- it will probably correct."
After Thursday's close, the CSCE reported certified coffee inventories fell by 4,000 bags, to 43,668 bags as of April 30. However, there were 7,227 bags of coffee pending grading, the exchange said.
The day's volume reached an estimated 13,192 lots.
